en: The Contemplation of the Five Aggregates, by the Śramaṇa Chengguan. Question:
An ordinary person who wishes to seek liberation—how should they practice? Answer: They should practice two contemplations. Second...

What are these two contemplations? First, the contemplation of the emptiness of persons; second, the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena. Indeed, the root of birth and death is nothing other than the dual grasping at persons and phenomena.

Because one is deluded regarding the general characteristics of body and mind, one grasps at the "self of persons" as being truly existent. Because one is deluded regarding the specific characteristics of the five aggregates, one reckons the "self of phenomena" as being truly existent.
Those who reckon a self of persons should employ the first contemplation to illuminate them, thereby knowing that the five aggregates are a mere combination.

One is provisionally designated as a "person. When one contemplates each [constituent] with true discernment, one sees only the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). One seeks the characteristic of a self or a person (*pudgala*), yet it is ultimately unobtainable. What are called the five aggregates?
They are form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). How does one contemplate them? The body is the aggregate of form.
These are what are called earth, water, fire, and wind. What are their characteristics? That which is solid is earth; that which is moist is water; that which is warm is fire;
that which is mobile is wind. When observing the mind, these are the four aggregates. What are their characteristics? Experiencing is sensation (*vedanā*);
grasping signs is perception (*saṃjñā*); conditioning is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); and cognizing is consciousness (*vijñāna*). If one can rely upon this body...

Regarding the characteristics of the mind: observe them clearly and discerningly. In all places, one sees only the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); when seeking the characteristics of a self or a person (*pudgala*), they are ultimately unobtainable.

This is called the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*). By relying on this contemplation, one practices and transcends the birth-and-death of the segmented realm (*bhavāgra-vedanīya-karma*), dwelling eternally in *nirvāṇa*;

this is called the liberation of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Those who reckon upon the self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) employ the subsequent contemplation to illuminate it, knowing that each and every aggregate arises from conditions.

All that arises is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); when the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) cannot be found upon investigation, then the five aggregates are all empty. This is called the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

If these two contemplations are illuminated simultaneously, one realizes that both the self of persons (*pudgala-ātman*) and the self of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*) are ultimately empty and non-existent, thereby becoming free from all fears.
It delivers one from all suffering and calamity. To emerge from the cycle of birth and death through transformation is called ultimate liberation. Question:

Now, seeking liberation simply means exhausting delusion and realizing the True. If one can merely accord with the quiescent principle of True Suchness (tathatā), then by being without thought, one will be freed from bondage.

Why resort to the contrived practice of contemplating the aggregates (*skandha*) to seek liberation? Is this not contrary to reason? Answer: Apart from the aggregates, upon what basis could the distinction between the true and the false be established?
Furthermore, the five aggregates are merely alternative names for body and mind. If a practitioner does not recognize body and mind, [how can they attain realization?]
How could the true and the false possibly reach a profound accord? Failing to comprehend the root of the true and the false, all conditioned practices are performed in vain.

Thus, a sutra says: "If one attempts this within empty space, it can never be accomplished. This is precisely what that refers to. Furthermore, to calculate a self in persons (*pudgala-ātman*) is the attachment of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);

to calculate a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātman*) is the stagnation of those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*). Therefore, one is made to cultivate the two contemplations; only then can one fully understand the false and realize the [true].
Truly. How could one ever be separated from it?
(End of the Contemplation of the Five Aggregates)
